comments.text: The boot file ROBOCOP loads here, at $0110, over the bottom of the stack, and starts with a BASIC line no one runs: 10 X=PEEK(186):LOAD"*",X,1, the usual way to load a program to its own address from the drive it came from

The boot file's code, reached through $0203 when the KERNAL's LOAD returns. Waits for raster line 11 and blanks the screen, sets a light blue border and blue background, turns KERNAL messages off, clears the screen, loads FAST from the same drive ($0169 sets the name) and calls it at $7000, then loads LOAD1 at its own address with the fast loader that FAST put in place, and jumps to $8000 to start the game
Sets the file name (length in A, address $01xx with the low byte in X) and the file: number $50, the drive the boot file came from ($BA), secondary address 1 so the file loads to its own address
File name LOAD1, padded with shifted spaces to 15 characters
File name FAS*: the wildcard finds FAST
The rest of the boot file: $02 bytes over the stack. When LOAD returns, the RTS pulls $02 $02 from here and goes to $0203, so the boot file starts itself without a RUN
The boot file's last six bytes, over the start of BASIC's input buffer: three more $02 bytes, then the JMP that the stack's return address lands on
Jumps to the boot code at $0128
The fast loader's computer side, put here by FAST. The five bytes M-E $62 $01: the disk drive's memory-execute command, which starts the drive half of the loader at drive address $0162
Jumps to the KERNAL's error entry at $F707, which reports error 5, DEVICE NOT PRESENT; $0A18 comes here when the drive does not answer

The LOAD vector at $0330 points here. Opens the drive's command channel and sends it M-E ($0A1A, five bytes through $FFA8) to start the drive's half of the loader. Patches $0A7D from the screen's vertical scroll ($D011), so the byte loop can tell which raster lines are bad lines, keeps the VIC bank bits of $DD00 in $94, turns sprites off while it loads, waits for the drive, and reads the file's load address
Keeps the load address in $AE/$AF: the file's own when the secondary address is not 0, otherwise the one in X and Y
Puts $99 (STA $0B00,Y) at $0AA5, so the loop below fills the block buffer. The BIT at $0A6A hides an LDA #$60 for the entry at $0A6B
Puts $60 (RTS) at $0AA5 instead, so the same loop returns after one byte, in A

Each byte: when the drive drops its line (bit 6 of $DD00) the block is over ($0AAC); otherwise waits for a raster line clear of the bad lines, where the VIC-II would steal cycles, signals the drive, and reads four pairs of bits from the clock and data lines of $DD00 on a fixed beat
This SBC's operand is patched at $0A2F from the vertical scroll, so the test skips the raster lines where the VIC-II steals cycles
This EOR's operand is patched at $0A41 from the VIC bank bits of $DD00, so they do not spoil the bits read
Stores the byte in the block buffer at $0B00, or returns it (see $0A66 and $0A6B)

A block is in: with the BASIC and KERNAL ROMs and the I/O chips switched out ($01 = $24), copies it from the buffer to its place in memory, so a file can load under them, then switches back ($01 = $27) and moves the load address on
When the load reaches $DB00, blanks the screen: clears bit 4 of $D011 on a raster line that matches
Waits for the drive; bit 7 of $DD00 says whether another block follows ($0A72). At the end puts the sprites back, sets the status $90 to $40 (end of file) and returns with carry clear: no error

The high-score table, eight entries of 18 bytes: three bytes of score in decimal digits, highest first (00 40 00 is 4,000), and 15 screen-code letters. LOAD1 brings it in and no level's files load over it, so it lasts until the machine is switched off; level three compares and inserts scores at $E93E-$E9CD. The names shipped with the game: ALIENATION, ANGST, MISERY, FRUSTRATION, TORMENT, DESPAIR, a row of dots, and HAVE A NICE DAY, all at 4,000 points
48 bytes after the table, inside LOAD1, that nothing reads

A tune that no code plays, left in LOAD1 after the bytes of level one's own: the end of its patterns, which run on from the leftovers at $B800, in the layout of the music driver's patterns, with pattern pointers that name these very addresses ($BF26, $BF2F), so it was built to sit here
From here to $BFFF the leftover changes to rows of eight bytes, probably the leftover tune's instruments; nothing reads them either

The status panel's screen in VIC bank 3, as LOAD1 brings it in: the message line ($C000-$C027), SCORE with its six digits at $C07F, the ROBOCOP logo, POWER with its bar of six characters at $C098, and the clock at $C0B2-$C0B5. The interrupt at the bottom of the screen points the VIC-II here (screen $C000, characters $D000) for the top of the next frame
The panel screen's eight sprite pointers, set to 5 by level one ($E08B)

Stage seven's tiles, used in level two: 143 of 4 by 4 characters, 16 bytes each, row by row. Level two's files do not hold them: they come with LOAD1 and wait here through level one, and level two's table at $E18B gives $C4 as stage seven's tile set. On the second disk image LOAD1 has other bytes here, and stage seven draws its walls from them
Stage seven's tiles 64 to 127
Stage seven's tiles 128 to 142, to $CCEF
The leftover code at $CD84 writes 1 here, inside what is now a tile
Six more tiles (143 to 148) that stage seven's map never uses
Code that nothing calls: turns four ASCII hex digits at $CD8A into a 16-bit number at $CD8F/$CD90, a piece of a development tool left in LOAD1
More leftover code: writes a space at $06FE+Y and steps Y back, then jumps to $CD09, where tile bytes now lie, so it belongs to an older layout of memory
The four ASCII hex digits the leftover code at $CD50 reads
Where the leftover code at $CD50 builds its number: the low byte here, the high byte at $CD90
The high byte of that number. From $CD91 to $CFFF the file holds what was in the authors' machine's memory: the stripes of $00 and $FF that the C64's RAM holds at power-on, with a few bits changed
More of the power-on pattern
More of the power-on pattern, to $CFFF
The rest of LOAD1 after level one's own bytes, to $FFF7: shapes laid out three bytes to a row like sprites, in the bank-3 sprite frames $F7 to $FE, which no sprite pointer ever names
